maintopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN U.K. DOLLAR IMPORTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN U.K. DOLLAR IMPORTS
speechtext:
I should like to inform the house that an announcement is being made in London today of a further major step toward the dismantling of the United Kingdom's restrictions on purchases from Canada and other dollar countries. Effective June 8, restrictions on dollar imports will be completely removed from some 110 items including a number not previously liberalized from non-dollar countries. In addition nondiscriminatory quotas will be established for 14 items for the next United Kingdom quota year. The existing dollar quotas for the current year will be enlarged for five other products. Most of the items on which controls are being removed can already be imported freely from western European countries and other commonwealth countries. This liberalization move represents an important and welcome measure of progress toward the elimination of discrimination against Canadian exports.
The steps which have now been taken by the United Kingdom are in accordance with the undertaking given by the president of the board of trade at the commonwealth conference in Montreal last September. At that time he said that all being well the United Kingdom would make a start this year with the removal of dollar restrictions on as wide a range of consumer goods and foodstuffs as possible. Most of the items affected by the latest liberalization move fall into these categories.
The products of particular importance to Canada which are now being completely freed from control include cheese, eggs, honey,
cereal breakfast foods, macaroni, canned soups and vegetables, paints, leather and leather manufactures including footwear, rubber manufactures including tires and tubes, hollow ware and hardware, wooden-ware and domestic electric appliances.
Canadian producers will have access to global quotas for such products as sporting goods, toys and games, stationery, clocks and watches and costume jewellery, fresh pears, canned apples and paper manufactures. Dollar quotas will be increased for other types of canned fruits and for motor vehicles.
Canadian producers of a considerable number of items formerly subject to discrimination have now been placed on a footing of equality with non-dollar suppliers in the United Kingdom market. This will open up new opportunities for the expansion of Canada's export trade, and will contribute to the desirable strengthening of trade relations between Canada and the United Kingdom.
We are pleased that at this time the United Kingdom government should have moved in this substantial way toward carrying out the program for the removal of dollar restrictions announced at Montreal. Discrimination will still remain with respect to quite a number of Canadian products, but we hope it will not be too long before we shall see the end of the restrictions against dollar goods which the United Kingdom and other sterling area countries have felt obliged to maintain throughout the post-war period.
We welcome the widening of markets which the dismantling of these restrictions will bring about. We welcome also the great improvement in the economic position of the United Kingdom which has enabled her to make sterling convertible and to proceed with the removal of artificial barriers to trade.
With the permission of the house I will table a list of the items which have been liberalized. I have four copies here; other copies will be available later this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN U.K. DOLLAR IMPORTS
speechtext:
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, we on this side welcome this news of further liberalization of trade between the United Kingdom and Canada. We hope this process will continue until all the discriminations which have existed for many years will have been removed. The process of removal has been going on for a long time.

Proposed Legislation
We welcome this move also because it is a reflection of the economic and financial strength of the United Kingdom itself. These considerations, of course, have been an obstacle in the way of liberalization over the years. We hope this liberalization can be extended not only to the United Kingdom but to the sterling area as a whole. I am thinking particularly of trade between Canada and the West Indies.
In so far as this represents a move toward the achieving of this final objective, I am sure all hon. members on this side will greatly welcome this announcement.

maintopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN U.K. DOLLAR IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any move that reduces trade barriers in the world is welcome. Since we all are quite aware that Canada is dependent for her prosperity to a very large extent on export markets, anything that is done to make it possible for Canada to maintain and increase markets is, of course, welcomed. The United Kingdom is an exceedingly important market for Canadian goods, and this is an additional reason why we are happy at the announcement that has been made.
We realize at the same time that it is becoming more difficult to maintain markets for Canadian goods. The European common market has raised certain difficulties. The government frequently refers to increasing competition from the U.S.S.R. which adds to the difficulties facing Canada today in the export and trade fields generally. We welcome this announcement as a move in the right direction.

speechtext: I take it that the minister has leave to table the document to which he referred?

maintopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN U.K. DOLLAR IMPORTS
speechtext: Agreed.

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill for the second reading of Bill No. C-49, to provide for the establishment of a national energy board, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Howard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking last night I was asked a question by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson), and was able to give him only part of the answer. In answering his question I referred to the fact that I was only a small fish in a large pool, and that when it is my turn to speak the big fish have usually left the pool. However, I am quite certain that if the Prime Minister is interested in my remarks, he can read Hansard for himself.
We have opposed and are opposing the national energy bill that we have before us. One of the reasons we are opposing it is that it is not a national energy bill. I should like to refer not only to the Borden commission report which we have heard quoted-and that commission did a survey of the energy prospects of Canada-but also to the report of the royal commission on the economic prospects of Canada under the chairmanship of Mr. W. L. Gordon.
In his submission on Canada's economic prospects he mentions a number of other forms
4108	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board of energy. I suggest that these other forms of energy must be taken into consideration if we are going to discuss an energy bill. I find that not only does he mention some of the ones that I referred to, but he also mentions some that I did not know about because I come from an inland area and therefore they do not affect me.
He points out at page 270 of the report of the royal commission that another form of energy is tidal power. He goes on to point out that in the maritime provinces, particularly at Passamaquoddy, a tidal power project has been discussed as a method of producing energy. This particular project must be national. It has been discussed by a national commission, a joint commission of the United States and Canada and they have discussed this matter since 1920. It is pointed out that this project, while physically feasible, is not necessarily an economic method of producing power at the present time. They point out at page 271 that in a joint commission report of 1950 the international Passamaquoddy tidal power project could be feasibly engineered, constructed and operated, and they go on to point out that it would be very expensive.
Another form of energy which I mentioned was nuclear energy. They pointed out some of the problems in the development of this form of energy, and also the fact that it was an important source of energy and would become much more important. Obviously if it is going to be a source of energy then it must be brought under the national energy bill if it is going to be truly national, and also take into consideration all forms of energy.
It also goes on to point out, as I mentioned last night, that there is a form of energy known as solar energy. I quote from the report at page 272:
Solar energy holds out hopes in quite a different direction. It falls on cheap waste land just as abundantly as on built-up areas in the nation's larger cities and towns. Solar operated devices can (and indeed must) be small in size.
As I pointed out, this will be effective in our northern development. It will be a factor in developing power necessary for expansion in our far north. These are some of the things that I think must be taken in consideration in a national energy bill, but they have been completely ignored.
Again, I think this bill is only a combination of a number of other acts that have been used to regulate the export of hydroelectric power and the sale, export and transmission of gas and oil. Canada has many other forms of national energy. It has many other energy resources which should also be given consideration. Many other important reasons have been given why this bill should


not be accepted and made final for the Canadian people. For this reason alone I suggest that the amendment should be supported and this bill be given the six months' hoist.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have read and studied the bill carefully, and I have also listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by various members during this debate.
I now rise to give, as it were, a summation of this group's point of view with respect to its hopes when the resolution was introduced; its disappointment when the bill was introduced into the house, and its alternative proposals to this legislation. In a way I am really concluding the remarks of this group on second reading and explaining our reasons for considering, shall I say, the aridity of this legislation. The embryo of this bill was buried in the very general language of the resolution preceding it.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that all my life I have been a bit of an optimist, and I had hoped that a healthy legislative child would be born with the introduction of this bill. We did not expect a very lusty infant, but we did expect that it would be healthy. However, our hopes were doomed to disappointment on the introduction of the bill.
Why did we have these hopes? Why were we justified in having hopes that this legislation would to some extent be satisfactory to the members of this group? Well, Mr. Speaker, first of all because the royal commission gave its close attention to the energy problem in Canada. It was a royal commission appointed by this government which, after an expenditure of over $300,000 of public funds, made its report to the government. It was on that account that we expected this government to give effect at least to the major recommendations of this report, and so did a great many Canadians across the country.
In addition, our hopes at the resolution stage were considerably bolstered by statements made by the Prime Minister when he was a member of the opposition in 1956, as well as statements of other prominent members of the present government at that time. Then again, we thought after the discussion in 1956 and the study of the whole situation by the royal commission on energy that the government recognized the need to protect the national and consumer interests of Canada by the creation of an effective national energy board. Here we have the introduction of a bill which does not even give a definition of what energy is.
In addition, we felt justified in expecting something because of the name given to the

board, the national energy board, in the resolution preceding this bill. However, Mr. Speaker, we were sadly disappointed with the undernourished orphan which was born when the minister introduced the bill into this house, and it was because of our disappointment that the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) moved this amendment which in effect would kill the bill at this time.
On the government side we have support for the bill. The Liberals have, shall I say, offered their tepid benediction to the measure in the dulcet tones of the official Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), in the cello-like resonance of the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer), and the piccolo-like sweet tones of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).

Mr. Speaker, I noticed during this debate that even the minister seemed to hang his head for the greater part of the time, and I noticed that on occasion he was peeping over at this group as much as to say, "Don't blame me entirely for this; it is not altogether mine." I could not help but think he looked like a shamefaced accoucheur in the introduction of this bill.
I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Macleod the evening before last with great interest. Apparently he speaks as a doctor of economics who has given some consideration to this measure. He has experience as a consultant in the oil and gas industry, and possibly has more understanding of the problem than a good many of his own colleagues. On that account I wish to quote a few passages from his speech which rather intrigued me and other members of this group, because if the speech is read carefully it was an expression of some doubt and concern. I now quote from page 4003 of Hansard of May 25, and this is what the hon. member said at that point:
There is one other point I should like to mention and that is that those who are charged with the responsibility of examining the contracts of the different companies should look into the question of escalator clauses in those contracts. I am told these gas exporting companies have escalator clauses in
National Energy Board
their contracts. In other words the price of gas is set at a certain level and then it goes up year after year in increments and gradually the price is increased. I have heard that these escalator clauses are based on economic trends. I would recommend to the government that they look into the question of who drew these economic trends. There is no other industry in this country that I know of that has escalator clauses in contracts relating to the things which it sets out to sell.
That is one of the reasons why this group is so concerned about an effective national energy bill. Then again the member went on, on page 4004, to say:
I believe that the economic forces should be bent in such a way that, over a long period of time, Canadian ownership will develop. Above all, we should maintain equity among the producers of gas and encourage Canadians to assume leadership in the production of gas and oil.
This is a clear admission that Canadians have not leadership in the production of gas and oil in this country at this time, and that is a situation this group is very concerned about. Then he went on to say, on the same page:
I now want to say a few words on another matter. I have been tremendously impressed by the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and of other members of the opposition and of the C.C.F.
So we have had some effect, you see, in this debate, Mr. Speaker. He continued:
They have gone to great lengths in praising the report of the Gordon royal commission which recommended the establishment of an energy board. The Gordon royal commission made the energy board their number one recommendation. You may be interested in knowing how that recommendation got into the report.
Mr. Gordon set up a system and asked for the help across Canada of scientists, economists and everyone whose services he could draw upon.
That is another reason, Mr. Speaker, why we object to this measure. The government has completely ignored the opinions and advice of this talented group of specialists in the field of the production of oil and gas, its marketing and so on. Then finally the hon. member finished his very interesting speech with these words.

I would not dream of doing that in any circumstances. But what did the hon. member for Macleod say, as reported at page 4005? He said, "The bill before the house is the best compromise that could be reached at this time." I am quoting in order to give a reason for this party's position. That is another reason why this group is opposed to this measure, because we consider it to be an unfortunate compromise which does not meet the needs of the Canadian national interest and the Canadian consumers at this time.
I was very interested to hear the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. McFarlane) with respect to the protests of certain municipalities in his constituency against the export of gas to the United States without the service being extended to the communities in that district. I support the hon. member wholeheartedly. Here is another illustration of the need for a board with effective powers. I have in my hand a copy of the Kimberley News of Wednesday, May 13 headlined "Kootenays seek Natural Gas-Ask Government Support" and I will quote briefly from the article in order to demonstrate the circumstances and the fact that the present authorities have no power to deal with these people; and as far as we can see, under this bill the national energy board will have no greater powers than those enjoyed by the present authority set up under the Pipe Lines Act.
Murray McFarlane, member of parliament for Kootenay East, will be requested to support a brief calling for the suspension of granting a gas export permit to Alberta and Southern Natural Gas until gas supply has been assured for the Kootenays.
The executive of the association of Kootenay municipalities-
Who, incidentally, sent me this paper.
-Friday night endorsed a brief to halt the shipment of 3,000,000,000,000 cubic feet of natural gas to the U.S.
Permission had earlier been granted to the company by the Alberta conservation board.
Dr. Fraser, commissioner at Creston will prepare the brief to be submitted to the federal government.
It was pointed out in a resolution presented to the executive meeting that the company is seeking an export permit from the dominion government to export the gas to the United States.


The pipe line crosses the southeast corner of the East Kootenays from Crowsnest at the Alberta boundary to Kingsgate at the Idaho boundary.
It has been pointed out that the communities of Fernie, Cranbrook, Kimberley, Chapman Camp, Marysville and Creston are all desirous of being served by natural gas.
The only way the Kootenays could obtain the gas would be from this planned export line which is not planned to conveniently serve them.
The resolution stresses the importance of the dominion government withholding the granting of a permit until the Alberta pipe line agrees to deliver natural gas to the boundaries of the East Kootenay municipalities at a cost comparable to which it is sold to the American pipe line companies at Kingsgate.
Fernie has already appeared before the Borden commission on the matter in a separate application.
If we had effective legislation there would be no necessity for these communities to present briefs to this government and go before commissions in order to get their natural right, the right to enjoy Canadian natural resources before they are exported to the United States.
This oil and gas industry is in my opinion a breed apart when it comes to dealing with governments at all levels and with consumers. That is indicated by my own personal experience. I remember when they were starting to build a pipe line across southeastern British Columbia, and the way some of the officials of the company concerned ignored the rights of citizens, or tried to ignore them, when it came to matters such as the location of the route of pipe lines, expropriation proceedings, compensation and so on, almost past belief. In a number of cases groups of citizens were obliged to organize and send representatives to Victoria. They were obliged to take co-operative and strong action in order to protect their rights, which should have been protected by law, either federal or provincial.
Again, when it comes to employment practices, these high and mighty people did not use the facilities of the national employment service in some districts in which they were operating. The manager of one of our employment offices in my own district told me that the engineer for one of these companies had said to him, "We are not going to use your potty little national employment service. We like a line-up at the office here every morning at seven o'clock so we can go along the line every morning and say 'You, and you, and you, and the rest can come back tomorrow' ". No other group of employers in southeastern British Columbia, in my experience, has taken that attitude and shown such complete disregard for Canadian rights, sensibilities and practices.
Then we come to the question of sales to the United States at lower prices than those which are being obtained in the province

*of British Columbia and other parts of this country and, in this instance, the complete disregard shown for the requirements and the wishes of municipalities which have been established for a long period of years and whose people have made a great contribution to the wealth of this country-places such as Cranbrook or Kimberley where the famous Sullivan mine is located. Consider the enormous wealth of products which come from that area; think of the lumber industry and the coal industry in the towns along the eastern end of Crowsnest pass. The requirements of these municipalities, the requirements of industry and the requirements of Canadian consumers will be completely overlooked unless we have an effective national energy board with powers to protect their interests.
I said previously that the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has moved this amendment, asking in effect for a six months' hoist for this legislation, because we believe that this bill does not give the board power to do the job it should do in order to protect the Canadian national interest and the interests of Canadian consumers. Here is a concrete illustration. This bill gives the national energy board no more authority than is exercised at the present time by the authorities who administer the Pipe Lines Act, if indeed it is to have as much. We intend to watch this situation very closely. What happens in the next few months with respect to the brief presented by the municipalities along the Crowsnest pass will determine very effectively whether the national energy board has the power to do the things which the minister says it can do.

This government, because of its political philosophy, is caught in the squeeze between the pressure and wishes of the industry and the need to do something to protect the national interest and the interests of Canadian consumers. The result is this compromise, this ineffective bill, this undernourished legislative orphan, this achromatic child of the government's dilemma.
When we offer criticism of the bill in all fairness we must offer constructive alternative proposals and I intend to outline briefly what a C.C.F. government would do under these circumstances.

Someone has commented that that is a hypothetical question. Only time will prove that there is more substance in my remarks than the hon. member gives credit for at this time.
What would a C.C.F. government do under the circumstances? First of all let me say there would be no conflict between the philosophy and policy of a C.C.F. government and the national and consumer interest. Therefore there would not be a necessity for compromise and rationalization in the introduction of a bill of this kind as demonstrated by the effective distribution of gas in Saskatchewan, which the hon. member for Assiniboia dealt with so ably in his reply to the remarks of the Prime Minister, who made a most unfortunate reference to Saskatchewan.
A C.C.F. government would establish a national energy board responsible to parliament and avoid the day to day interference by the governor in council made possible under this bill. We recognize from attending various committee meetings this session the serious position of the Canadian economy in respect of international trade, and the necessity to do all that is possible to effectively meet increased competition.
One of the prime requirements in effectively meeting foreign competition in trade is low cost power effectively distributed across the country. A C.C.F. government would give effect to a national policy along the following lines. The national energy board would have
4112	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board power to make recommendations to parliament with respect to public ownership that could best serve the national and public interest under various circumstances obtaining in Canada. That would be considered primarily in respect of the interprovincial transport of oil and gas. The board would be given power to protect the national consumer interest in the export of gas. It would not issue licences under which companies could sell gas in the United States at prices below those obtaining in respect of Canadian consumers.
A C.C.F. government would establish a board that would promote policies designed to conserve and direct the use of energy resources. A C.C.F. government would establish a board with power to ensure that, as far as is practicable, fuel and power resources were equitably distributed to all sections of the populated area of Canada. A C.C.F. government would establish a board with power to introduce rates and charges for the transportation of power in its various forms whether that energy was being transported under public or private ownership. A C.C.F. government would establish a board with power to co-ordinate the activities of various agencies having information that would assist in the development of energy resources whether on the federal or provincial level or in private industry.
A C.C.F. government would appoint a board with power to promote research into every field of the production, distribution and marketing of energy in Canada. A C.C.F. government would establish a board with power to work in co-operation with a dominion-provincial advisory energy council so that the activities of the board within the provincial sphere could be correlated and the rights of provincial jurisdiction would be respected. It would ensure that all activities were directed to the end of an ample supply of cheap power equitably distributed throughout Canada.
I have dealt with our hopes and disappointments, and have briefly outlined what would be the policy of a C.C.F. government if it were appointing a national energy board and introducing legislation of this type at this time. In our opinion the present bill is a legislative facade that provides the opportunity for the government to accept the credit for any small advantages that may accrue, and to place the blame for its disadvantages on the shoulders of the national energy board. It is a hollow shell, and for that reason the hon. member for Skeena has introduced his amendment which we shall support.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my
intention to speak at any great length at this stage of the debate on second reading because I realize that the house generally is eager to get into the committee stage where the bill can be dealt with clause by clause. I appreciated the remark of the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition (Mr. Pearson) last night when he said, "We are trying to get this legislation through."
I prefer to refer to him as leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition and not leader of the official opposition. He is obviously the official leader flanked by aspiring and unofficial leaders. But as leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition he has co-operated to the extent of indicating that the house in general is anxious to get this legislation through and certainly to the committee stage so that there can be careful study of the various clauses.
In the course of the debate, although it was on the general principles of the bill, as it developed the principles were at times overlooked and certain extraneous material was introduced. But just to remind the house, I think it should be clearly set out that, as far as general principles are concerned, this
National Energy Board bill is to establish a national energy board which shall, in order to assure to the people of Canada the best use of energy resources in this country, regulate in the public interest the construction and operation of oil and gas pipe lines subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, the tolls charged for transmission by such pipe lines, the export and import of gas, the export of electric power and the construction of those lines over which such power is exported. The board shall also study and keep under review all matters relating to energy within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and shall recommend to the Minister of Trade and Commerce such measures as it considers necessary or advisable in the public interest with regard to such matters. The bill also authorizes the extension of the export and import provisions to oil.
In the course of my opening remarks on second reading I set forth the principles with which we are concerned. I might say here, Mr. Speaker, that I do not intend to deal with the remarks of each hon. member who participated in the debate up to this stage. I appreciate the valuable contributions made by many of those who took part, but so many of the points raised have reference to various clauses of the bill that it would seem advisable to deal with those suggestions and criticisms as the clauses come before the committee.
However, I notice that in some of the statements made by members of the opposition there was criticism to the effect that this bill did not go far enough in that it was not concerned with all forms of energy in Canada. In my opening statement I attempted to make it quite clear that we were not interfering with the dominion coal board and that we were not attempting to take over the functions now performed so adequately by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited but that we were concerned with the question of electricity, oil and gas, the export of those forms of energy and the import of them when necessary.
In the bill we have made provision for wide advisory functions of the national energy board so that board can advise the government as to the policy that might be pursued with regard to energy and the sources of energy. The opposition stressed the point that this bill should be referred to a standing committee, a suggestion which is hard to balance against their repeated statements that there is nothing new in the bill, that it is simply a continuation of policies which they have advocated in the past and which they had placed on the statute books. In

National Energy Board view of those statements, it is hard to understand why they would now want to refer this bill to a standing committee for further study.
They have referred to the work of the Gordon commission. They have commented upon the Borden commission. From both those careful investigations of energy in Canada surely sufficient information is now in the hands of the house for it to proceed with this bill without further reference to one of the standing committees. The committee of the whole house is quite competent to deal with it.
A great deal of attention was given by some hon. members of the opposition to the alleged seizure of arbitrary powers on the part of the government. This is a strange change of attitude on the part of my hon. friends opposite. It shows that they have learned something from the debates that took place in this house in 1955 and 1956 to which they have made reference and from which they have quoted at some length. I think they have learned in part the lesson that was taught them in those days. However, it ill befits them now to suggest-as was suggested by one member of the opposition, namely the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith)-that closure was being attempted in this debate. Nothing of the sort is being attempted. The debate is wide open for any length of time that people desire. There is nothing in the nature of any seizure of arbitrary powers. Everything is disclosed in the bill. We have placed it before the house for consideration. Every aspect of it can be examined. We have no intention now -and never have had any-of wanting to do anything without the authority and consent of parliament.
They have directed their attention particularly to clause 87 which we have set in there subject to later proclamation. That is not an unusual course in connection with bills that come before this house. That course of action has been followed on many occasions in the past. It permits the house to examine the proposition, to give its consent -or withhold it, if it so desires-and then having the facts disclosed, permit the subsequent proclamation of a section or sections of the act when the time seems propitious for that to be done. There is no concealment here or no intention of taking any arbitrary powers. If it seems advisable at some subsequent date to proclaim section 87, the document which does that will be immediately tabled in the House of Commons and debate permitted with regard to that action.

speechtext:
Hon. members of the C.C.F.
party made a lengthy, if somewhat raucous, contribution to the debate and ranged extremely far afield. I am surprised to find them aligned in opposition to national development and to the establishment of a national energy board.
In the debate which took place in this chamber in February of 1957, and which has been referred to frequently by hon. members opposite, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), who was then leader of the opposition, introduced a resolution advocating national development and in the course of his speech proposed the setting up of a national energy board, the C.C.F. party of that day, under its then leader, supported that resolution and supported the idea of national development and found no objection to the setting up of a national energy board.
But the present surviving members of what was once a strong party of this house have taken a stand against national development and against a national energy board. On the one hand they have advocated nationalization of pipe lines, public ownership, and on the other hand they have suggested that if there is to be a national energy board it should have complete powers without any responsibility to parliament, a misunderstanding surely of the function of parliament and how the executive is responsible to parliament. As I followed their argument through its devious course, it appeared to me that they were advocating some body which would be completely independent of this parliament. That is not the type of body that we are setting up. We are setting up a body which is responsible to the government, which in turn is responsible to parliament. Every action of that board and every action of the government is subject to question and review.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: It is just a pawn of the cabinet.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. group, who speaks not in the measured tones of his distinguished predecessor of a few years ago, says it will be a pawn of the cabinet. That is not true. Like any other body set up by parliament it will report to the cabinet and it will report through the Minister of Trade and Commerce to parliament, and every action taken will be reviewed. I do not see the purpose that is attempted to be served by the C.C.F. party in the attitude which they have taken with regard to this bill. The wisdom of the house is of course against them on the two motions we have had before this house. The house has voted them down and has pressed on with the consideration of this particular problem.
We are prepared, Mr. Speaker, in the committee stage to examine very closely all angles of what I have earlier said is a very complicated problem. There is no pretense that this question of dealing with energy and the sources of energy in Canada is not complicated. It ranges far afield and involves not only matters within our own country and the conservation of our resources but our export policy, our relations with our neighbour the United States, and all sorts of difficulties which arise in dealing with oil and gas in particular.
In conversations with members of the federal power commission in the United States which have been conducted over the years by officials of the department, a great deal of advice and information has been received as to the difficulties which confront boards charged with responsibility such as we are proposing to give to the national energy board. We appreciate the difficulties that are ahead, and it is for that reason that so much of this bill has been drawn in general rather than specific terms, so that the national energy board comprised, as we expect it will be, of men of experience and ability will, in the general framework which will be set out, be able to map out a policy which will be in the general interest of all Canadians. Experience over the course of the next 12 months will guide us in the future, but this is a step in the right direction. This, as I said on the introduction of the resolution, is the fulfilment of a policy pursued by this party over many years.
As the Prime Minister mentioned, the suggestion of a national energy board to deal with Canada's national development was proposed by the late Gordon Graydon many years ago, and subsequently that idea was carried forward year after year through debates in this house sponsored by the Conservative party. The setting up of the national energy board at this stage is part of
Division
the fulfilment of our desire to develop the resources of Canada in the interests of all Canadians, and we are confident that through the bill which is now before the house, and subsequently through the board which will be set up, the interests of Canadians will be protected, that our resources will be adequately developed, and Canada will continue to maintain her position as one of the leading nations of the world.
The bill which is before the house setting up a national energy board I am sure will meet with general approval throughout this country. We have already had indication that there is general approval for action of this nature which is in line with the policy of national development announced by this party and now being followed through on many fronts. No front is of greater importance to the Canadian people than that which relates to energy, and the national energy board will fulfil the purpose that we have had in mind over the years.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was pointed out that this group believes that this bill is 
not properly referred to in the first clause. A national energy board should be empowered to deal with energy in all forms whereas this bill establishes a national energy board in respect of the regulation of gas and oil only. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Timmins:
That clause 1 be amended by deleting the word "Energy" and substituting the words "Gas and Oil Regulatory".

speechtext:
Is
the committee ready for the question?

speechtext:

On clause 2-Definitions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: There are so many subparagraphs to this clause that I wonder whether it is the intention of the minister to deal with them as one clause or one by one? I have some remarks on several parts of the clause. It would be more orderly if they were dealt with one by one.

speechtext:

Subclauses (a) and (b) agreed to.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Can the minister make clear the origin of this definition of "company" and explain the difference in the definition from that contained in the previous legislation?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the Pipe Lines Act "company" is defined in section 2, subclause (b) as follows:
"Company" means a person having authority under a special act to construct or operate pipe lines for the transportation of oil or gas.
There is no change there except that we said, "To construct or operate pipe lines".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The point I want to make is that it appears that by adopting the definition contained in this subclause the minister is striking out any differentiation between company pipe lines and other pipe lines. Can he develop that, or explain why it has been done?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
There is no intention to
make that distinction. In the Pipe Lines Act, chapter 211 of the Revised Statutes of Canada a company pipe line was defined. We dropped that and here we define a company and later we define a pipe line.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: What I am seeking to point out is that there is a difference in the definition here from the former legislation. There was a difference between a company pipe line and a pipe line. That distinction seems to have been dropped. I am not arguing that it should or should not be dropped. I would like the minister to tell the committee why this distinction has been dropped. What is the effect of it?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps I did not make it clear. It was a separation of the definition. The company pipe line in the Pipe Lines Act was explained rather fully, and what we have done is to split the thing, to define "company" as I read it out just a minute or two ago and then to define "pipe line" on page 2, incorporating the relevant phrases that occur in the Pipe Lines Act. It seemed to us to make it clearer to drop the expression "company pipe line".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Pipe Lines Act contains a definition of the word "company", then a definition of "company pipe line" and then a definition of "pipe line". The effect of that was to have two classes of pipe lines, the company pipe line and then the other pipe lines that were included in the definition "pipe line" and which were not company pipe lines. That distinction has been dropped. There must be some reason for it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think we have it clarified by the present definition, Mr. Chairman. The explanation that has been put forward is that under the old act a pipe line could include things other than the movement of oil or gas. It might be for the movement of water or salines, liquids, and things of that nature.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before you proceed to pass the definition of "company", may I say I read this to mean that it includes a crown corporation, if one were established to operate a pipe line. Is that so?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That appears to be correct.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, not only that but it excludes other companies that may be operating pipe lines because of the fact they were operating much earlier than the enactment of the Pipe Lines Act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Can the minister explain how under this act a company can mean a person? No permits will be granted to companies. It would seem to me that one person is singled out in this subclause, which is definitely not the intention.
National Energy Board

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: In the Interpretation Act a person includes a company. This is just a reprint from the Pipe Lines Act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: No, it is not a reprint. It omits part of the definition in the Pipe Lines Act. It is not a reprint; it is a reprint of part of it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Can the minister explain to the committee why a company would not include a corporation, and so on, which would have a licence under the legislation which we are about to pass for the Canadian people concerning the administration of energy in Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would repeat that question? I missed part of it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The clause as it now stands
is not in conformity with the previous act from which apparently it comes by way of the scissors and paste method. The bill simply states that "company" means a person having authority under a special act to construct or operate pipe lines. Why should it no be more specific and indicate what bodies or entities may be considered as companies to whom we may grant permits, further extend permits, refuse permits and so on?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I thought that the explanation of that was in what I said earlier about the Interpretation Act.

Subclause agreed to.
On subclause (d)-Export.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Will the minister explain the origin of this definition?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is the definition in the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act in so far as power is concerned and, quoting from that act, the definition of "export" is as follows:
"Export" means
(i) with reference to power, to send from Canada by a line of wire or other conductor.
That portion of the definition in the bill comes from the Exportation of Power and Fluids and the Importation of Gas Act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am concerned with the second part of subclause (d). I take it that is new. Is that correct?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is new because of the use of the word "hydrocarbons" instead of the word "fluids".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
What I want to get some explanation of is this. Under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas
4118	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board Act the term "export" was defined, and the definition in so far as power is concerned is the same in the bill as in that act, but with reference to fluids the definition of the word "export" is wholly changed. The definition in the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act dealing with fluids reads as follows:
"Export" means-
(ii) with reference to fluids, to send from Canada through pipe lines or other like contrivances.
In other words, there are two limitations there. The export of oil under these regulations was confined to the export of oil through pipe lines, and that is the only oil under control under that act. That was the point I sought to make with respect to the Prime Minister's remarks on second reading. When he addressed the house he dealt with this subject but he did not make any reference to the limitation contained in that act and, indeed, in remarks he made during the course of the debate yesterday the Minister of Public Works was guilty of the same omission.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that there is no export by any other means than pipe lines?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am seeking to clear up what might very well be a misleading impression created by the Minister of Public Works when he stated, if I remember correctly, that there had been the right to control exports since 1907. I sought to point out by way of interjection, which, of course, is a poor way to do it, that control was limited to export through pipe lines. In other words, it was an attempt to control pipe lines and, indeed, it came into force in 1907 at a time when there was no question of export. The problem of finding markets for oil simply did not exist then. That was the point I wanted to make.
I thought that the minister should clear up the matter here because otherwise it could be very misleading.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: In recent years the pipe line method of moving oil has been almost universally accepted, and as far as Canada is concerned that is the way it is moving instead of by tank car or truck. There can be export by these other means and we have made allowance for that but normally export is by pipe line.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The point I wish to make is that export by pipe line, of course, obviously refers only to export to the United States and by means of that one method only. The bill is sharply different. Contrary to the argument made by the Prime Minister and implied by the Minister of Public Works, the export control now sought by the minister is sharply different in that it involves export 

by any means. That is the whole crux of the argument. I do not see why that is not admitted and put forward in that way by the government. I do not see why there should be an attempt to be confusing with respect to it.
It is quite clear that any control or regulation with regard to the export of oil was limited by that definition to export through pipe lines which means export to the United States by one method only and that there was not control of export by tanker or any other method which would imply, of course, export to other countries and which could become important now that this country is in the fortunate position that the oil industry has developed. There is a big problem to be faced in finding markets. It is a wholly different problem and I think the minister should clear up this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Ottawa West misunderstood the exchange between the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate and myself. He was complaining about the government taking arbitrary powers and so on and so forth and I asked him if he was not aware that since 1907 there had been control over the export of oil. That was the basis of the question and it was asked because he was criticizing us for taking control over the export of oil. Then he admitted that the former government had this control, and in effect they had control over all export of oil because oil was only exported by pipe line.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think I can let the
minister get away with that argument because in fact there was only authority to control it through pipe lines and if there was any other practical method of shipping oil to any other country by any other means it was not under control. In other words, what was sought to be controlled in 1907 was the subject of pipe lines, not the subject of the export of oil. Our problem today is quite different. We are seeking to find markets for oil. I think the minister will agree that at that time the problem arose because of the necessity for control of the export of electricity. That is the point I want to make.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, under this subclause the definition of "export" so far as hydrocarbons are concerned is unlimited, in other words, "to send from Canada by any means" but in a subsequent subclause, subclause (g) which deals with imports, the definition of "import" in its application to gas and oil is limited to specified methods of importing. Would the minister explain why this distinction was made with regard to the definitons of "export" and "import"?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition is quite correct. The definition has been spelled out when we are dealing with imports in subsection (g). There the idea was that if a license procedure had to be adopted for imports of oil, it would not apply to small quantities which might come in by other means than those there specified. Under the question of export and sale by any means, it was not spelled out in the same way in view of the fact that, if the control of the export of oil was under consideration, there might be substantial exports by other means -or it would include gas-not foreseen at the present time which perhaps should come under control.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Then paragraph (d) which deals with export means that if oil were brought in by air freight it would not be subject to control because it would not be imported.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am not sure that the definition would apply there. There may be other methods unknown to us by which these things could be transported.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: There is another point to be made clear with reference to export, namely that the government is seeking a sharp widening of any control there may have been in the past on two grounds. Formerly it was obvious that export control could only apply to the United States because it was through a pipe line. That is the first ground. The other is as to quantity. If by any chance they make export control regulations applicable by the act under the later section, then they are going to be controlling any quantities of oil to any country in the world. I am wondering just how far this matter has been thought through by the government and to what extent they intended so sharply to extend the export control as they are doing through this method of definition.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I might point out that sections 82 and 83 give a certain amount of leeway here for exemptions and these exemptions could be applied in the case of small quantities or quantities that were not of any great importance. Section 85, subsection 2 indicates another exemption regulation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That has to do with the regulations. The government is taking extremely wide power here and is asking for much wider power than was indicated in any of the speeches made on the second reading of this bill. It is quite true that they may say, "Maybe we will not take as wide power as we are asking for", but it is not in the act. Parliament has not passed on that matter at all. Parliament had the
National Energy Board limitation in the earlier legislation; it does not have it at all in this legislation. Parliament had imposed its limitation in the earlier legislation; in this case parliament is asked to remove all limitations on the subject. That is the point I wish to make.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as to the reference made by the minister to section 82 may I say this. Does not the word "exportation" in section 82 (a) refer to the definition in clause 2 (d) and therefore are we not back to the same problem?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was drawing attention to subsection 2 of section 82 which reads:
(2) A licence issued under this part may be restricted or limited as to area, quantity or time or as to class or kind of products.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Surely the minister is not expecting the board more or less to over-ride the cabinet and parliament as to what they will decide in the very elementary problem of what under this act it is meant for them to govern.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Nothing of the sort.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: We do not find in the definition anything as to the responsibilities of the board. The minister refers the house to paragraph 2 of clause 82 and states that there they have more or less vague and unlimited powers to deal with areas and modes of transportation and that they will have in their own fashion the right to distinguish as to what is meant in the extremely important matter of this act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: What I was objecting to in the hon. members' statement was this. I think he said something to the effect that the board would act without reference to parliament. If he will read section 82 again, he will notice it states "Subject to the regulations", and the regulations have to be approved, as will be seen by reference to section 85. In all instances these regulations will have to be approved by the governor in council. Hence the board is not simply given a free hand. Their authority would be spelled out in the regulations.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the minister indicating to the house that in the final analysis it is for the cabinet and the governor in council to decide all matters under this act?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not know. If the hon. member wants to interpret it in that way it is within his rights as a matter of this house to do so; but it is not the interpretation that we put on it. Even in those acts which we are now supplanting by this one, regulations were passed spelling out some of the

National Energy Board sections of those acts and giving instructions as to what should be done with regard to licences, fees, export, import and so on.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: There is one other point I wish to refer in connection with clause 2 (d). I refer to the definition in (d) (ii) "with reference to hydrocarbons, to send from Canada by any means". I have dealt with the point "by any means" being an enlargement over the former provision "by pipe line". As to hydrocarbons-we shall come to that matter separately-the terms has reference to oil and gas. The former act had to do with fluids and the definition of fluids included gas, oil, water or any other fluids and so on, exported by way of pipe line. I want to ask the minister just what other fluids, if any, are exported from Canada by pipe line, whether water or otherwise. Second, I should like to ask this question. If any water is exported from Canada, a matter which was regulated under the former legislation, what provision is made for the regulation of it now? Is it being dropped from all regulations? If so, why? The point turns on the definition of the word "fluids" in the former legislation and its omission in this legislation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: In the old act having water in there meant that licences had to be issued for saline solutions and woodpulp in aqueous suspension. These are not going to be required under this act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Will they be regulated under any other federal regulations or legislation?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is derived from the definition of fluids under the act, a saline solution and wood pulp in aqueous suspension.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: As I understand it, that legislation is repealed?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Then does that mean there will be no regulatory control over such export at all?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Not under this, because they were not sources of energy and therefore are not included here.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: But as I understand it, that act is repealed by the new one.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: It will be.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The whole of that act is being repealed by the bill now before us?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I would like to find out from the minister if it is the intention of the government that such saline and wood pulp solution as now being exported by means of pipe line and under regulatory control will cease to be under regulatory control?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: If that control is now being exercised it will cease when the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act is repealed, and it is not our intention to impose any regulatory control.

Subclause agreed to.
On subclause (e)-Gas.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Subclause (e) is a new definition altogether. Would the minister give an explanation of that?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, that is a new definition. It brings in temperature of 60 degrees fahrenheit and pressure. The definition of gas refers to laboratory conditions and has nothing to do with the temperatures or pressures at which such hydrocarbons are normally carried or transmitted in commerce. The principal reason for such a definition, apart from convenience and the fact that gas and oil must be separated in some way, is that it was considered desirable to control the import of propane and butane into Canada, and to do this they must be classified as gases since the bill provides for the immediate licensing of gas imports but only for the contingent licensing of oil imports. Propane and butane are normally transmitted in liquid form, but under conditions of normal temperatures and pressures are gaseous and must fall under the regulations.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Then I take it that the definition of gas would include propane and butane as presently transported; is that the intention?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: One other question, and I am not sure whether this comes under the definition of gas or hydrocarbon. Perhaps I could leave it until we get to hydrocarbon.

Subclause agreed to.
On subclause (f)-Hydrocarbon.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I have two points on this. There was a pipe line company incorporated this session, but unfortunately I have forgotten the name of it at the moment. It had to do with a proposition to export certain material, if I may call it that for the moment. I think the minister will be familiar with the company I am referring to. Does the product proposed to be put through that pipe line come within the definition of either hydrocarbon or gas as defined in this legislation?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The answer to the hon. member's question is that it is not included in this definition.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is, it is not included in either the definition of gas or oil, and therefore it would not come under this legislation at all; is that right?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Well, not at this stage. Subsequently, when we reach a clause further on in the bill I will draw attention to this and we will bring to the attention of the committee that that type of operation would come under a portion of this legislation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps I can let it go. Am I to understand from that that it is not the intention of the government that such international pipe lines should be freed from control?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: There will be a minimum of control with regard to that type of pipe line which is not carrying an energy or a source of energy. At the same time we do not want to exclude from some of the provisions of this bill certain advantages which might come to a pipe line of that sort if it came under this legislation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: What I want to draw to the attention of the minister at this point is that such a pipe line is in the minds of the public, at least in areas of Canada where there are no big producers of oil, in exactly the same situation as an oil or gas pipe line with all the implications that that has with respect to the public financing of the company, and so on. I am just wondering as to the wisdom of the government freeing such an operation from control, with the careful type of hearing which is giving the public protection. I refer to the type of hearing that the board of transport commissioners has been giving to these cases, and which, I presume the new board will also give to these cases. It seems to me it is an innovation which should at least have been mentioned on second reading.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to the Foothills Pipe Lines Ltd., is he not?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, that is it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Which has been incorporated under Bill No. S-16 of the Senate of Canada. I judge that full opportunity was provided to obtain all the information which was being required with regard to the matters he has indicated in connection with the incorporation of a company of this nature.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my concern did not have to do with the incorporation of the company at all. My concern had to do with the fact that by the definitions we are now adopting as to gas and hydrocarbon in relation to this present bill now before us we are exempting from the type of control which formerly existed under the Pipe Lines Act
National Energy Board certain proposed very large international pipe lines dealing with the export of one of the oil industry by-products from western Canada. The implication of that is pretty serious because the whole concept at the time the Pipe Lines Act was enacted, and I think as is the intention with this bill, was to control those large interprovincial and international pipe lines. There was inherent in that legislation, as there is in this, a certain measure of protection in that the applicants had to come before a board-in the former case the board of transport commissioners, and in this case the national energy board-and give a great deal of information as to the economic soundness of their proposed operation. There is a long list of criteria which they have to prove before those boards, and as well as proving economic soundness in the sense of having a sufficient supply of the product to put through the line, and a sufficient market for it there was the requirement of this board for full information about the proposed method of financing so that anyone really concerned could find out exactly what the method of financing a line was to be-how much was to be debentured and bond debt, and how much was to consist of other types of capital; what the equity capital was and so on.
By taking such pipe lines outside the operation of the act we are really being asked to embark on a wholly new policy. Before we turn to clause 3, there were two other matters outstanding with regard to clause 2. The first had to do with the omission of any definition of the word "energy", and the omission is significant

in the light of the use of the word "energy" in the latter part of the bill.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right. I was asked why energy is not defined. It is used in the bill only in clause 22 in the part dealing with the advisory functions of the board. It was thought wise not to limit it by definition. There can be no misunderstanding of the subjects with which the board will be dealing as it continues its study and review of matters pertaining to energy and sources of energy. Sources of energy not now in use may be discovered or developed as time goes on, and there seems to be no necessity therefore to define and, by that means, to limit the meaning of "energy".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: On that point, I draw the attention of the minister to the fact that clause 22 is mandatory. It charges the board with the responsibility of studying and keeping under review matters concerning energy and sources of energy in Canada. There are a great many sources of energy in Canada which I am sure it is not the government's intention that the board should be obliged to study and keep under review. That is the difficulty into which the minister is heading by omitting to define the term "energy".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think that although the
board is expected to study these matters and keep them under review it will not in its wisdom devote time and effort to unproductive subjects. I think we can trust the board to relate its work to what is generally understood by the words "sources of energy" and "energy".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: The point I am making is that the board has no opportunity to exercise its wisdom in this respect. The legislation charges it with the responsibility to study and keep under review matters relating to energy and sources of energy. The board has no discretion to exclude certain sources of energy from its considerations. It has no authority for excluding them. That is the consequence of proceeding without a definition of the word "energy". I think it is reasonably clear from the course of this debate so far that the minister and the government have in mind that these studies shall pertain to certain well known sources of energy-oil, gas, coal, atomic energy and so on.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
What was in our minds was that the regulatory functions of the board would relate to electricity, gas and oil. But the study and review would relate to energy and sources of energy, and the board could range as widely afield as it wished, the purpose being that it should inform itself with
National Energy Board reference to these matters and be in a position to advise the government. We did not wish to place any restrictions on the board in this connection and we leave it to the judgment of the board as to the intensity of their study and the extent of their review in any particular direction.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: My point is that the board is not left with any discretion in the matter. Following the minister's argument, either clause 22 must be changed or there must be a definition of "energy". The board cannot keep under review only those sources of energy which it thinks best deserve study. The hon. gentleman must either define the word "energy" or adopt the recommendation of the Borden commission relating to clause 22. He cannot have it both ways.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not see the matter in quite the same light as the hon. gentleman. There is an opportunity for the board to use its discretion. Part (2) of clause 22 states:
The board shall, at the request of the minister, prepare studies and reports on any matter relating to energy or sources of energy.
These would be matters to which they had already given study and which they had had under review, but more detail might be required by the government.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Paragraph (2) of clause 22 is discretionary, and the discretion lies with the minister. But paragraph (1) of clause 22 is mandatory and requires the board to include all energy and all sources of energy in its studies.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps we might take the example of solar energy which has been mentioned during the debate. Solar energy has not yet advanced through the stage of experimentation to the point where it is competitive with other fuel sources. The board will take cognizance of what is being done in relation to the harnessing of solar energy, but would not need to spend too much time on it at this stage. It will keep itself informed of what is happening and advise the government accordingly. Surely there is room here for the board to decide, in its wisdom, which subjects should receive long and detailed study, and which subjects should be given more limited consideration.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
