Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the committee will not agree that, notwithstanding his good intentions, the minister has really not dealt with the suggestion on its merits, that instead of a board of five there should be a board of three in accordance with the recommendation made by the Borden commission.
The Prime Minister told us, I think the day before yesterday, that since becoming Prime Minister he had been surprised to find out how difficult it was to persuade good and competent people to leave their private occupations and take on responsibilities of this kind. If there was much merit in the observation of the Prime Minister, that argument ought to be rather convincing in the context of the situation that is now before the committee. In addition to this, the minister has the example of the unemployment insurance commission of three members, a body that administers a very large fund and has very many heavy administrative responsibilities. I think the board of broadcast governors is limited to three but there is a large executive committee. I may be wrong in this one but my impression is that there are three consisting of Dr. Stewart and two others and they are assisted by a large executive committee. It would seem to me that, in addition to the reasons given by the hon. member for Gloucester, there is the third argument of efficiency and of preventing unnecessary expenditure, the great purpose to which this government was dedicated certainly in the days of elections and presumably in the days of actual responsibility not so much so.
I suggest to the minister that this is a good suggestion and that in the absence of a satisfactory explanation as to why it should not be accepted the minister should accept it. He has the opportunity at the moment of explaining, in addition to the reasons he has already given, further reasons, but unless he can establish clearly the necessity of having five members it seems to me it is not unreasonable to accept this suggestion. The consequential changes that will be required in the remaining subclauses of the clause can be dealt with simply by editorial revisions. They do not involve any fundamental obstacle to the suggestion as made that we ought to follow the pattern with regard to bodies of this sort that the federal government has established. Commissions of three have worked well. They provide for adequate representation of occupational interests, and I strongly suggest that the minister will find it not as difficult to appoint three as five if we are to take seriously the observations made
4132	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board by the Prime Minister. In any event, the minister owes us a much more complete reply than that which he has given.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I am very happy to add to the explanation that I gave earlier. In the first place, let me point out and repeat that the Borden commission did not limit the number to three. It suggested three and not more than five. Second, the energy board will deal with one of the greatest industrial developments in Canada. The oil and gas industry is in its infancy and the whole development of energy and sources of energy in Canada is on the threshold of great advances. This board will be heavily engaged in dealing with one of the most vital parts of the Canadian economy. To limit the board to three members might incapacitate it from performing its function fully because there is always the chance of a member being away or ill. There is also the necessity for this board to do a certain amount of travelling throughout Canada and to hold hearings in various parts of the country. Furthermore, my hon. friend talks about having a board of three. He overlooks the fact that the board of transport commissioners is a board of six members. I do not recall that during his term in office he suggested that it be reduced for the purpose of economy.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.

There are other reasons which might be advanced to persuade my hon. friend of the weakness of his argument. I am glad he recognizes that we are interested in economical operations, but there can sometimes be false economy when you do not provide the proper number of people to carry out a job of major importance. From the experience of our friends across the border we know the difficulties they have had in an industry which has grown by leaps and bounds in that country, and which will grow by leaps and bounds in Canada. The work of the energy board will become increasingly onerous as the years go by.

It has jurisdiction over matters in the United States which in this country are reserved for provincial governments.
If the federal power commission can get along with a board of five to deal with matters of far greater scope than those to come under the board provided for in this legislation, surely a board of three would be just as effective in doing the work as a board of five and would save a good many thousands of dollars a year. I am the more convinced of that, because the regulatory functions of a board of that kind, as anyone realizes who knows anything about the operations of administrative boards, can be performed as well by three men as by five, and in some cases perhaps better by three men.

He spoke about the difficulty of getting competent members on a board of this kind and the difficulties of having adequate compensation, and that sort of thing. I was tempted, as a matter of fact, to suggest to him at the time that there are other factors in getting the best possible board, and one is that the board, since it is a court of record, should be given independence to carry on its own work within the ambit of the bill and not be interfered with or dictated to. There is a good deal to be said on the subject about why members of these boards are leaving. I for one am perfectly frank in admitting that I am concerned about the number of able men who have left various boards within the last few years. I think of boards such as the board of transport commissioners, the Canadian farm loan board and the tariff board. There is a real problem for the government there

in the loss to the public service of Canada of men of the calibre who have left those boards.
The point I want to make arises out of the Prime Minister's remarks on page 4025 of Hansard for May 26 last. He was dealing at that point with certain Alberta applications, and I would like to quote a passage from what the Prime Minister said in order to make my point. In referring to these applications he had this to say:
In so far as those applications are concerned, they will be processed immediately by the board when it is set up. It will be set up immediately. There will be no need to wait for the mobilization of the board. The members of the board, from the evidence taken by the Gordon commission, the evidence taken by the Borden commission and the evidence taken by the conservation board of Alberta, will be in a position, I am sure, to determine fully the entire question.
The point I want to make is that the minister gave a firm commitment as to what the board would do. He did not indicate that he would ask the board to undertake the matter immediately, to deal with these cases immediately, and have the necessary hearings, or as the case may be. Not only that, but he went further. He undertook to indicate what evidence the board could deal with. That is a pretty serious matter. If you are setting up a board which will be a court of record, and then before the board is set up limit the evidence it can hear on particular applications, it is indeed quite shocking and I am sure not what the Prime Minister intended had he thought about it. I think he has had enough court experience to realize the impropriety of that course, and I would hope that the minister at some point in dealing with this matter will clarify the position and make it perfectly clear that there will be no such dictation to the board as is indicated in the remarks I have quoted. I regret that the Prime Minister is not here himself to deal with the point, because I am sure he could not have realized the extent to which he went in those remarks in the form in which they appear in Hansard. They appear to be absolutely ordering the board as to what they shall do, and even determining what evidence they shall consider in certain cases which will be coming before them in the future. I think it is a point which should be made very clear before any members are appointed to the board, or indeed any persons are approached to be members of the board.

Clause 4 in subclause (1), calls for certain salaries to be paid to the chairman, vice-chairman and members of the board. We are not questioning those salaries, because we realize that if we want to get men to do the job which they are called upon to do under this bill they must be paid accordingly. But when we come to subclause (2) stating that expenses shall be paid to the members of the board, we certainly have some questions to raise. The subclause reads:
Each member is entitled to be paid reasonable travelling and other expenses incurred by him in the performance of his duty while away from his ordinary place of residence.
We know that according to subclause (7) of clause 3 members may reside a distance away from Ottawa, as the governor in council determines. This leaves an opening for unwarranted expenses and we feel that a firmer control should be imposed over this board as far as travelling and other expenses are concerned. I therefore move:
That subclause (2) of clause 4 be amended by replacing the words "his ordinary place of residence" by "the city of Ottawa".
It should be remembered that this board is called upon to sit in Ottawa, and for this reason we feel that the amendment should be accepted.

speechtext: The answer to that question is: yes-a very dogmatic yes. Though I may say it was not under the Railway Act.

Under the bill we are now considering the ordinary place of residence may be


St. John's, Newfoundland or Vancouver, and every time a member of the board comes to Ottawa for two days he would be able to claim expenses.

speechtext: I wonder if the minister would offer a word of explanation about the phrase "and other expenses incurred by him" in subclause (2) of clause 4. maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I think we should have a better explanation from the minister than the one he has given. After all, it has been said that this board is called upon to sit in Ottawa. I think this is simply running the risk of incurring unnecessary expense and we are warning this government which has committed itself to avoiding all unnecessary extravagance of the possible consequences. I want to recall to the government as well that at present there is an inquiry going on in certain committees about travelling and moving expenses. That is a warning to the minister. I think he should take it in good faith and accept this amendment.

speechtext:
